source.paraphrase: Prefer unknown when a value's type is not yet known. any disables the checker for everything it touches.

invariants.why: any turns off checking for every value that flows through it. Banning it is a project type policy, and strict libraries still use it at boundaries, so the default contract leaves this check off. Opt in with an override severity of warn or deny.
invariants.fixHint: Give the value a named type, or accept unknown and narrow it before use. If a third-party payload truly has no schema, put pregate-allow-any: and the reason on the comment directly above that statement.
invariants.avoid: A marker inside a string, or a marker above an earlier statement, does not cover a later any. as unknown as T is a different escape and is still a cast.

source.paraphrase: Use the type checker to prove a switch covered every member of a union. A default that accepts never fails the build when a member is added.

invariants.why: A union that gains a member stays compilable when the switch has no exhaustiveness check. Requiring a throw, return, or never in default is a prescribed shape, so the default contract advises.
invariants.fixHint: Add a default that assigns the remaining value to never and then throws or returns it, so a new union member fails the build.
invariants.avoid: default: break compiles and does nothing. A nested switch's default does not count for the outer switch.

source.paraphrase: A postfix ! tells the checker to assume a value is present. That assumption is unchecked at runtime.

invariants.why: A non-null assertion is a local claim that a value is present, not proof that it is absent. Strict code uses it after a check the syntax rule cannot see, so the default contract leaves this check off. Opt in with an override severity of warn.
invariants.fixHint: Narrow with a conditional, use optional chaining and a fallback, or change the callee so it does not return null.
invariants.avoid: Writing the assertion twice (value!!) is still an assertion. !== is a comparison, not this operator.

source.paraphrase: Prefer a union of string literals to an enum. The union does not emit a reverse mapping, and each member is its value.

invariants.why: A numeric enum invents a reverse map. A string enum is still valid TypeScript, so banning every enum is a style choice and the default contract leaves this check off. Opt in with an override severity of warn.
invariants.fixHint: Replace the enum with a union of string literals, and keep the list next to the function that switches on it.
invariants.avoid: const enum still declares an enum. It only changes emit. A union is the replacement.

source.work: TypeScript handbook, strict boolean checks, and Google TypeScript style
source.paraphrase: Conditions should be booleans. Do not rely on the truthiness of a number or a string when the comparison can be written.

invariants.why: A length or a literal used as a condition hides the comparison. Using length as a condition is idiomatic JavaScript, so the default contract advises.
invariants.fixHint: Compare length to 0, or name a boolean. Leave a plain identifier alone when the checker cannot see the type.
invariants.avoid: if (!!items.length) is still a length used as a boolean. if (items.length > 0) is the comparison.

source.paraphrase: Explicit public function annotations are an optional boundary policy. TypeScript also supports contextual inference, so inferred inner callbacks and annotated function-valued exports are valid.

invariants.why: This optional public-boundary policy requires explicit parameter annotations on directly exported TypeScript functions, including defaulted parameters. TypeScript correctly infers limit = 25 or now = new Date(). The default contract leaves the check off. Opt in with an override severity of warn. A finding does not prove implicit any or a type-checker defect.
invariants.fixHint: Write limit: number = 25 or now: Date = new Date(), or annotate the exported function-valued variable. Keep inferred implementation callbacks unchanged. If inferred public defaults are the project policy, propose a scoped override or replace this optional style check with a compiler assertion; do not add impossible TypeScript annotations to JavaScript.
invariants.avoid: Only .ts/.tsx/.mts/.cts parameters directly owned by a directly exported function or an unannotated exported function-valued variable are checked. Inferred literal and constructor defaults still require annotations under this selected policy. Nested callbacks, annotated function-valued variables and plain JavaScript are allowed. Re-exported declarations, class members and shorthand single-parameter arrows require compiler evidence; this syntax rule does not replace noImplicitAny.

source.paraphrase: Prefer readonly for data other modules can see, so a change has to go through an operation that returns a new value.

invariants.why: A mutable field on an exported type lets any caller reassign data the owner thought it controlled. Requiring readonly on every public property changes library APIs, so the default contract leaves this check off. Opt in with an override severity of warn. Options, config, and input bags stay exempt either way, because marking them readonly would reject legal construction of the public API.
invariants.fixHint: When the project opts in, add readonly to properties of exported data the caller must not mutate. Leave options, config, and input types mutable.
invariants.avoid: The syntax check covers properties in directly exported interfaces, type aliases and explicit function/method signature annotations, including nested public types. It skips a directly exported interface or type alias whose name starts or ends with Options, Config, Configuration, or Input, including OptionsInit and RetryOptions, and nested properties of that type. Executable bodies, runtime assertions and runtime call type arguments are implementation context. Marking one public field readonly does not cover the next. Class field declarations and a non-exported type followed by export { Type } require additional compiler evidence.

source.paraphrase: For application code, ES modules replace namespaces. A namespace is an older container that merges across files.

invariants.why: A namespace merges values and types in a way modules already express. Namespaces remain valid TypeScript, including for declaration merging, so the default contract advises.
invariants.fixHint: Move the values to a module and export them by name.
invariants.avoid: export namespace is still a namespace. A class or a plain object does not need one.

source.paraphrase: Don't use the types Number, String, Boolean, Symbol, Object or Function. They refer to boxed objects or untyped callables. Use number, string, boolean, symbol, object, and specific function types.

invariants.why: A boxed type names an object wrapper the code almost never holds, Object accepts every primitive, and Function accepts any callable without parameter or return type safety.
invariants.fixHint: Write string, number, boolean or symbol. Replace Object with object, unknown or a named shape, and replace Function with a specific signature such as () => void.
invariants.avoid: Generic constraints and type arguments are type positions too. Value calls such as String(x) or Object.keys are not types. A global interface String augmentation and a qualified name such as Wire.Object are allowed.
